child_care.agency: Minnesota Department of Children, Youth, and Families (DCYF), Licensing Division
child_care.licensing: Anyone operating a nonresidential child care program (care outside the child's home for less than 24 hours a day) needs a DCYF license unless excluded by law (Minn. Stat. §142B.05); centers follow Minn. R. ch. 9503, and school-age child care programs (more than 10 children, mainly school-age care) and drop-in programs are licensed as centers with some special rules (§142B.41, subd. 6).
child_care.school_age_exemption: Excluded from licensing (Minn. Stat. §142B.05, subd. 2): programs run by a public school for children 33 months or older; school-age programs run by a school, YMCA, YWCA or JCC; park and recreation board programs; scouting, clubs, sports and art programs; nonresidential programs running fewer than 30 days total in 12 months; qualifying nonprofit youth development programs for grades K-12 that give parents written notice they are unlicensed; religious instruction; and youth camps licensed by the Department of Health. Excluded programs that take child care assistance funds must be certified as license-exempt centers (ch. 142C).
child_care.ratio_rule: Minn. R. 9503.0040, subp. 1; Minn. Stat. §142B.41, subd. 6 (school-age programs)

camps.agency: Minnesota Department of Health, Food, Pools and Lodging Services Section
camps.summary: The Department of Health licenses youth camps, defined as camps that provide both food and lodging (overnight) for 10 or more people for 5 or more days a year; its rules cover the site, sanitation, food, water, health care and first aid (Minn. Stat. §§144.71-144.74; Minn. R. 4630.2300-4630.4700). Day camps without lodging are not youth camps under that law; they need a DCYF child care license unless they fit a licensing exclusion (for example park and recreation programs, sports or art programs, nonprofit youth development programs, or programs running fewer than 30 days a year).

background_checks.summary: Child care center staff and others with direct contact need a state background study that includes fingerprints for a national (FBI) criminal check, Minnesota criminal and predatory offender records, Minnesota maltreatment records, the national sex offender registry, and criminal, sex offender and child abuse registries in every state lived in during the past five years; the study must be repeated within five years (Minn. Stat. §§245C.04, 245C.08). No background check requirement was found in the state youth camp rules (Minn. R. ch. 4630).

medication.summary: A center that chooses to give medicine needs written parent permission (also for diapering products, sunscreen and insect repellent) and written instructions from a physician or dentist for each prescription; a current pharmacy label counts as instructions. Medicine must be in its original container labeled with the child's name, never given past its expiration date, stored out of children's reach, and every dose recorded with the child's name, medication, date, time, dose and the signature of the person who gave it (Minn. R. 9503.0140, subp. 7).

mandated_reporting.summary: Professionals and their delegates in child care, education, health care, social services, mental health, corrections, probation and law enforcement, plus clergy, must report (Minn. Stat. §260E.06); anyone else may report. Reports go to the county or tribal social services agency or law enforcement immediately by phone, followed by a written report within 72 hours (excluding weekends and holidays) (§260E.09).

child_care.agency: Mississippi State Department of Health (MSDH), Child Care Facilities Licensure Branch
child_care.licensing: A license is needed for any place that cares for six or more unrelated children under age 13 for any part of the day. This covers day care centers, preschools, school-age programs and summer day camps unless an exemption applies. Homes caring for five or fewer children can register voluntarily, and homes caring for 12 or fewer children in the operator's home have their own regulations.
child_care.school_age_exemption: Programs run inside an accredited elementary or secondary school are exempt. Accreditors include the Mississippi Department of Education, SACS, the Mississippi Private School Association, AACS, ACSI and Accelerated Christian Education. Also exempt: programs that run three weeks or less a year (such as vacation Bible school or scout day camps), care offered no more than two days a week as respite, and national membership groups such as Boys & Girls Clubs or the YMCA that charge only a nominal yearly fee ($600 or less) and meet their national standards (Miss. Code Ann. § 43-20-5).
child_care.ratio_rule: Miss. Admin. Code Title 15, Part 11, Subpart 55, Ch. 1, Rule 1.8.2 (ratios) and Rule 1.8.3 (group size); school-age group sizes repeated in Rule 1.22.3

camps.agency: Mississippi State Department of Health (MSDH), Child Care Facilities Licensure Branch
camps.summary: Overnight youth camps need an MSDH youth camp license under the Mississippi Youth Camp Safety and Health Law (Miss. Code Ann. Title 75, Ch. 74). This applies to camps on a permanent site running four or more consecutive 24-hour periods for 20 or more children aged 6 to 18. Athletic camps and hunting or fishing camps are excluded. Day camps are generally covered by child care licensing, which has specific summer day camp rules (Rule 1.22), unless an exemption applies, such as running three weeks or less a year.

background_checks.summary: All operators, employees and prospective employees of a licensed child care facility need a comprehensive fingerprint-based check before starting work. It covers the FBI and Mississippi criminal history, the state child abuse registry, the national and state sex offender registries, and other states when applicable. Staff can't start until MSDH issues a Letter of Suitability. The check is repeated every five years, and again after a break in service of more than 180 days. Volunteers who work 120 or more hours a year need the same check (Rule 1.5.2). The MSDH youth camp regulations do not include their own background check requirement.

medication.summary: The child's file must hold a parent's signed written authorization to give medication (Rule 1.6.7), and the facility's written procedures for storing and giving medication must be shared with parents before enrollment (Rule 1.4.1). Each dose must be logged with the date, time and the signature of the staff member who gave it (Rule 1.6.3). Staff who give medication must be able to read the directions and dispense it correctly (Rule 1.5.1).

mandated_reporting.summary: Miss. Code Ann. § 43-21-353 lists professionals, including child caregivers, school employees and ministers, and then adds 'any other person' with reasonable cause to suspect abuse or neglect, so everyone must report. The report must be made right away by phone or otherwise, with a written report following as soon as possible.

child_care.agency: Missouri Department of Elementary and Secondary Education (DESE), Office of Childhood, Child Care Compliance and Regulation
child_care.licensing: Anyone caring for more than six children, or more than three children under age 2, must be licensed by DESE unless exempt (RSMo 210.201, 210.211). License types are family child care homes (up to 10 children), group child care homes (up to 20) and child care centers.
child_care.school_age_exemption: Several programs are exempt under RSMo 210.211: school systems, summer or day camps run in good faith mainly for recreation, programs serving only children in grade 6 or above, neighborhood youth development programs, and child care under the exclusive control of a religious organization. Any program that receives state or federal child care funds (other than USDA food program funds) cannot claim an exemption, and unlicensed programs must tell parents in writing that they are not licensed.

camps.summary: We found no Missouri state license for youth camps. Summer and day camps run in good faith mainly for recreation are exempt from child care licensing (RSMo 210.211.1(4)). A 'day camp' runs between 6 a.m. and 7 p.m. when local schools are not in session, and a 'summer camp' runs May to September (RSMo 210.201). Both serve children 5 and older in kindergarten or above and can't share space with care for younger children. A camp that receives state or federal child care funds can't use the exemption.

background_checks.summary: Before working, child care staff must have a qualifying result on a check that includes an FBI fingerprint check, the national sex offender registry, and the criminal, sex offender and child abuse/neglect registries (including the Family Care Safety Registry) for Missouri and every state lived in during the past five years. New staff may start on a temporary eligibility notice if they are supervised at all times. Checks are repeated every five years (5 CSR 25-600.010 and .020; RSMo 210.1080). We found no separate state requirement for exempt camps.

medication.summary: Providers don't have to give medication, but if they do they need the parent's dated written permission stating how long it may be given. Prescription medicine must be in its original container labeled with the child's name, instructions and physician's name, and over-the-counter medicine in its original container labeled by the parent. All medication is stored out of children's reach or locked. Each dose is recorded with the date, time, amount and name of the person giving it (5 CSR 25-500.192(3)).

mandated_reporting.summary: RSMo 210.115 lists required reporters, including day care center workers and other child-care workers, teachers, principals and other school officials, health and mental health practitioners, social workers, ministers, law enforcement, and any 'other person with responsibility for the care of children'. They must report to the Children's Division immediately. Anyone else may report.

unverified: DESE is rewriting its child care licensing rules under Executive Order 25-15 and held informational sessions on proposed changes in March-April 2026. The official rule chapter we used is the Secretary of State's December 2023 code update. Ratios or other rules may change once new rules are filed.

Two 2026 bills (HB 3142 / SB 1642) proposed regulating overnight and residential camps. HB 3142's last action was 'postponed' on April 21, 2026, and RSMo 210.211 still shows the camp exemption (version effective August 28, 2024). We didn't confirm SB 1642's final status.
There may be no state license for overnight (resident) camps at all. We found none, but no official source states this directly.

child_care.agency: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS), Early Childhood and Family Support Division, Child Care Licensing Program
child_care.licensing: Any provider regularly caring for seven or more children must be licensed or registered. Child care centers (16 or more children in an out-of-home setting) must be licensed. Group homes (9-15 children) and family homes (7-8 children) must register (ARM 37.96.102).
child_care.school_age_exemption: School-age care facilities, which serve only school-age children during out-of-school time, and drop-in facilities may choose to be licensed but are not required to be (ARM 37.96.102(3)(a)(i)). DPHHS says before-school, after-school, drop-in and preschool programs do not need a license.

camps.agency: Montana DPHHS, Environmental Health and Food Safety Section (with local environmental health offices)
camps.summary: Montana licenses 'youth camps' under Title 50, Ch. 52, MCA and ARM 37.111 subchapter 12. A youth camp is land with buildings, tents or other structures used as living quarters for 10 or more people, mainly for minors' education or recreation. The license covers sanitation (water, sewage, solid waste and food service), not staffing or programming, and applications go through the local environmental health office. Day programs without living quarters don't appear to be covered. Programs for school-age children may choose to be licensed as school-age care.

background_checks.summary: Directors, owners, teachers, substitutes, trainees, support staff, volunteers with unsupervised contact and adults living in the facility need satisfactory checks before working (ARM 37.96.1002). The checks are a Montana DOJ/FBI fingerprint check, the national (NCIC) and Montana sex offender registries, child protective services checks, and name-based criminal checks for Montana and every state lived in during the past five years. State checks are repeated every year and national checks every five years. We found no separate background check rule for youth camps.

medication.summary: Staff may give medication only with the parent's written authorization, which must list the child's name, how long it applies, dosage amount and time, and the parent's signature. Medicine must be labeled, and prescription medicine kept in the original pharmacy-labeled container. All medicine is stored out of children's reach with child-protective caps, and expired medicine can't be used. Programs that give medication keep a log of the date, time and dose (ARM 37.96.502).

mandated_reporting.summary: MCA 41-3-201 lists required reporters, including teachers and school employees, operators and employees of registered or licensed day-care and child-care facilities, health and mental health professionals, clergy, social workers, law enforcement, and employees of groups that contract with DPHHS to serve children. They must report promptly to DPHHS. Anyone else may report.

child_care.agency: Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), Division of Public Health, Licensure Unit (Child Care Licensing)
child_care.licensing: Child care for four or more children at a time generally needs a DHHS license under the Child Care Licensing Act (Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 71-1908 to 71-1923). Rules exist for Family Child Care Homes I and II, child care centers (13 or more children), school-age-only centers (13 or more children in kindergarten or above) and preschools (391 NAC chapters 1-5).
child_care.school_age_exemption: Exempt programs include services offered only to school-age children during summer and other long school breaks, programs run or contracted by a public school district under State Department of Education rules, recreation camps (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 71-3101), and recreation programs run by a city, county or other local government. Care averaging less than two hours a week and care only for children 13 and older are also exempt (391 NAC 3-001.02 and 4-001.02). Exempt programs may still choose to be licensed.

camps.agency: Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), Division of Public Health (environmental health)
camps.summary: Recreation camps need an annual DHHS permit to operate under 178 NAC 1, Rules and Regulations Relating to Recreation Camps. The rules mainly cover the campsite, buildings, water, plumbing, sewage, food, swimming pools, safety, first aid and health records. Recreation camps are exempt from child care licensing. A summer-only program for school-age children is also exempt from child care licensing.

background_checks.summary: Under the center rules, the licensee, every staff member and volunteer aged 19 or older (and household members if the center is in a home) need a criminal history check before employment, through the Nebraska State Patrol or local law enforcement. Everyone must also clear the Nebraska child abuse/neglect central register (age 13 and older), the adult protective services registry (18 and older) and the State Patrol sex offender registry before caring for children (391 NAC 3-006.03). The recreation camp rules contain no background check requirement.

medication.summary: Staff may give prescription or over-the-counter medication only with prior written permission and written instructions from a parent, following the 'Five Rights' (right drug, child, dose, route and time). A prescriber's written statement is needed for as-needed prescriptions or unusual routes. All medication is kept locked in its original container labeled for the child, and the time and amount of each dose is recorded. Errors must be reported to the parent (391 NAC 3-006.27).

mandated_reporting.summary: Nebraska requires any person who suspects child abuse or neglect to report it, not only listed professionals. Reports go to law enforcement or the DHHS hotline. Center directors must immediately report, or make sure a report is filed, with the Child Abuse-Neglect Hotline and/or local law enforcement (391 NAC 3-006.02).

child_care.agency: Nevada Division of Social Services (DSS), Child Care Licensing (CCL)
child_care.licensing: A state license is required to care for more than four children who are not your relatives, or for whom you are paid, under NRS and NAC Chapter 432A. License types include family homes (up to 6 children), group homes (up to 12), child care centers (13 or more), out-of-school-time programs, accommodation facilities and institutions. Cities and counties may also require business licenses or special use permits.

camps.summary: We found no Nevada state license or permit specifically for youth day or overnight camps. 'Outdoor youth programs' are a separately licensed category under NAC 432A.630-.780, but those rules focus on clients' treatment plans and psychological oversight, not general recreation camps. A day camp serving school-age children 10 or more hours a week may count as an Out of School Time program under child care licensing, so check with DSS.

background_checks.summary: Every employee, and every resident or volunteer aged 18 or older (other than a parent of an enrolled child), must be fingerprinted within 24 hours of being hired or first being present, and again every five years. The state reviews criminal history and any substantiated child abuse or neglect reports (NAC 432A.200). New hires are entered in the Nevada Automated Background System (NABS). We found no state background check rule specific to camps.

medication.summary: Prescription medicine must be in its original container with a child-proof lid, plainly labeled with the child's name and locked up or kept out of reach. Except in an emergency, only one person chosen by the licensee and trained by a health professional or the child's parent may give medication. A written record of each medication, child, date and time is kept in the child's file (NAC 432A.376).

mandated_reporting.summary: Nevada lists the professionals who must report (NRS 432B.220), and child care licensees and employees must report suspected abuse or neglect under that law. If the abuse may be happening in the facility, they must also report it to the licensing division (NAC 432A.410). Report to the county child welfare agency for your area.

child_care.agency: New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), Child Care Licensing Unit (CCLU)
child_care.licensing: CCLU licenses family child care homes, family group child care homes, group child care centers, child care nurseries, preschools, school-age programs, night care and residential programs under RSA 170-E and He-C 4002. A private home caring for its own children plus up to four others is exempt.
child_care.school_age_exemption: Exempt programs include those run by a public or private school or college; skill-instruction programs such as athletics, crafts, music or dance; and municipal recreation programs, including after-school and summer programs. Also exempt are recreational programs for children 6 and older run by a school, religious group, Boys & Girls Club, Girls Inc., YMCA or YWCA, if they notify parents they are unlicensed, have a grievance policy and meet national standards (RSA 170-E:3). Exempt programs serving children on a state child care scholarship must still meet certain health and safety rules, including background checks.
child_care.ratio_rule: He-C 4002.35 (group child care centers); He-C 4002.38 (school-age programs)

camps.agency: New Hampshire DHHS, Child Care Licensing Unit, Youth Camp Program
camps.summary: Youth recreation camps, both residence camps and seasonal or year-round day camps, need a DHHS license (RSA 170-E:56; He-C 4003). This covers programs running at least 10 days a license year for 10 or more youth a day. Programs licensed as child care, or exempt from child care licensing under RSA 170-E:3, I, don't need a camp license. 'Youth skill camps' (a set curriculum over 3 or more consecutive days) are not licensed but must run criminal background checks on anyone who may be alone with children.

background_checks.summary: Child care staff, substitutes, other employees, volunteers who may be alone with children or count in ratios, and household members 18 and older need a background check before starting and every five years (He-C 4002.40; RSA 170-E:7). The check covers NH criminal records, the NH abuse/neglect registry, the NH sex offender registry, an FBI fingerprint check, the national sex offender registry, and other states lived in during the past five years. Staff can't be with children until CCLU confirms eligibility, apart from supervised presence after clean fingerprint results. Youth recreation camp staff need criminal checks in every state they have lived in, a national sex offender registry check, an NH central registry check if they lived in NH in the past seven years, and references (He-C 4003.17).

medication.summary: Only trained, authorized staff (or a nurse or licensed practitioner) may give medication. They need a medication order (a prescription label or a licensed practitioner's order) plus the parent's written permission. Staff must complete medication training before giving any medicine and again every year. Medicine stays in its original container and out of children's reach, each dose is logged with the date, time and staff signature, and parents are told immediately of any error (He-C 4002.20).

mandated_reporting.summary: Any person who suspects that a child under 18 has been abused or neglected must report it immediately to DCYF (RSA 169-C:29-31). Proof isn't required, and DCYF may ask for a written report within 48 hours.

child_care.agency: New Jersey Department of Children and Families (DCF), Office of Licensing
child_care.licensing: Any home or facility that cares for six or more children under 13 for less than 24 hours a day needs a DCF child care center license. That includes school-age child care programs and recreation-type centers run by county or municipal recreation or park departments. Family child care homes (five or fewer children) are not licensed; they may register voluntarily.
child_care.school_age_exemption: Exempt from licensing: programs run by a local public school board; programs that are an integral part of a private K-6 school; single-activity programs such as sports, art, music or dance (limited to 2 hours a day for children under 6); qualifying homework/tutoring programs; and youth camps holding a Department of Health youth camp license. Drop-in programs of 2 hours or less with the parent in the building, and 'open door' programs where children come and go on their own, are not centers. Sources: N.J.A.C. 3A:52-1.2 and 1.3.

camps.agency: New Jersey Department of Health, Youth Camp Safety program
camps.summary: Private day camps and resident (overnight) camps need an annual youth camp certificate of approval from the Department of Health under the Youth Camp Safety Act (N.J.S.A. 26:12-1 et seq.) and N.J.A.C. 8:25. A youth camp serves five or more children under 18 for two or more days in the same week; a day program with only a minimal recreational part and no high-risk activity is not a camp. Municipally run camps are not required to be licensed, and a licensed youth camp does not also need a DCF child care license.

background_checks.summary: Licensed centers: the sponsor and every staff member working on a regular schedule must consent to a Child Abuse Record Information (CARI) check, resubmitted with each license renewal, and the sponsor and staff 18 and older must complete a fingerprint-based criminal history (CHRI) check through the State Police and FBI. New staff must start both within two weeks of hire and cannot be left alone with children until results arrive (N.J.A.C. 3A:52-4.10, 4.11). Youth camps have their own rule (N.J.A.C. 8:25-3.2): adult staff with unsupervised access need a 50-state name-based criminal check (resident camps also need an FBI fingerprint check), all staff need an annual sex offender registry check, and full checks repeat every five years, with the first deadline June 15, 2026.

medication.summary: Centers must tell parents their medication policy at enrollment and give medicine only with the parent's written approval, by designated trained staff. Medicine stays in its original container (prescriptions labeled for the child) in a locked or inaccessible place, each dose is logged, over-the-counter medicine is limited to listed types given per the label unless a health care provider authorizes otherwise in writing, and school-age children may self-administer with written parent authorization under staff supervision (N.J.A.C. 3A:52-7.5).

mandated_reporting.summary: Every person who has reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused or neglected must report it immediately to the Division of Child Protection and Permanency (N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.10). Reports can be anonymous; call 911 as well if a child is in immediate danger.

child_care.agency: New Mexico Early Childhood Education and Care Department (ECECD), Child Care Services Bureau, Regulatory Oversight Unit
child_care.licensing: ECECD licenses child care centers, out-of-school-time (OST) programs for school-age children (ages 5 to 18, before and after school or when school is out), and licensed family and group child care homes. A person caring for four or fewer non-resident children in their own home is exempt from licensing (8.9.4.9 NMAC).
child_care.school_age_exemption: The licensing rules do not apply to programs run by a public school system and governed by the local school board; accredited private schools serving children 5 and older for education only; summer camps, wilderness camps and recreation-only programs run by recognized organizations such as churches, schools and scouts (if not in a private residence); summer religious schools; and care where parents stay on the premises (8.9.4.9 NMAC). Other before/after-school programs need an OST license.

camps.summary: We found no New Mexico youth camp license. Summer camps, wilderness camps and recreation-only programs run by recognized organizations (churches, schools, scouts) are exempt from ECECD child care licensing as long as they are not in a private residence (8.9.4.9(G) NMAC). A day program for school-age children that does not fit that exemption may need an ECECD out-of-school-time license.

background_checks.summary: All staff, volunteers and anyone with unsupervised access to children in licensed centers and OST programs need a comprehensive check: fingerprint-based state and FBI criminal history, state and national sex offender registries, New Mexico abuse and neglect records, plus criminal, sex offender and abuse/neglect checks in any state lived in during the past five years. A person may not start until cleared or issued a notice of provisional employment, and must be directly supervised until cleared. Checks repeat at least every five years (8.9.6 NMAC; 8.9.4.21 and 8.9.4.40 NMAC). No separate camp requirement was found.

medication.summary: Medicine may be given only with written permission from a parent, following the prescriber's written directions (or the parent's written instructions for over-the-counter products, including sunscreen and insect repellent). A designated staff member gives it from the original container labeled with the child's name and date, keeps it locked, signs a log of each dose that the parent initials the same day, and never gives expired medicine (8.9.4.26(C) NMAC). New staff must complete approved training that covers medication administration within three months of hire (8.9.4.23 NMAC).

mandated_reporting.summary: Every person who knows or reasonably suspects a child is abused or neglected must report immediately to CYFD Statewide Central Intake, local law enforcement, or the tribal agency for an Indian child in Indian country (NMSA 32A-4-3).

unverified: No New Mexico youth camp licensing law or rule was found, but this could not be ruled out completely; resident camps may still need Environment Department permits for food service, pools or water systems (not confirmed).
ECECD posted proposed amendments to 8.9.4 NMAC in June 2026; adoption status not confirmed. Ratio tables in the proposal match current rules.

The State Records Center HTML copy of 8.9.4 NMAC shows amendments only through Oct. 8, 2024; the Nov. 4, 2025 amendments were checked in ECECD's PDF and did not change ratios, medication or five-year re-check rules.

child_care.agency: New York State Office of Children and Family Services (OCFS), Division of Child Care Services; in New York City, child care centers for children under 6 are permitted by the NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
child_care.licensing: OCFS licenses child day care centers (seven or more children, more than three hours a day) and group family day care homes. Family day care homes, small day care centers (three to six children) and school-age child care programs (more than six school-age children) register with OCFS instead (Social Services Law §390). In New York City, center-based care for children under 6 needs a NYC Health Department permit under Article 47 of the NYC Health Code; school-age programs in NYC still register with OCFS.
child_care.school_age_exemption: Not child day care, so no license or registration: day camps as defined in the State Sanitary Code; after-school programs run for religious education, sports or recreation; and kindergarten, pre-K or after-school programs run by a public school district or a private elementary/secondary school on its own premises (Social Services Law §390(1)(a)).
child_care.ratio_rule: 18 NYCRR 418-1.8(k) (child day care centers); 18 NYCRR 414.8(k) (school-age child care programs)

camps.agency: New York State Department of Health (Subpart 7-2 of the State Sanitary Code); permits are issued and camps inspected by the local health department (the NYC Health Department in New York City)
camps.summary: Summer day camps, traveling summer day camps and overnight camps need a permit from the local health department and are inspected twice a year. A summer day camp, for this rule, serves children under 16 between June 1 and September 15 with organized activities, at least one of which is a non-passive recreational activity with significant risk of injury (10 NYCRR 7-2.2). Programs that do not meet the camp definition are not permitted as camps; summer programs may instead be run by OCFS-licensed child care programs.

background_checks.summary: Prospective child care employees, directors, operators and volunteers with potential unsupervised contact need state (DCJS) and FBI fingerprint checks, a Statewide Central Register (child abuse) database check, New York and national sex offender registry searches, and criminal, sex offender and child abuse registry checks for any other state lived in during the past five years. Clearances must be repeated at least every five years (Social Services Law §390-b). Children's camps: camp directors undergo background checks and operators must check staff and volunteers against the New York State and national sex offender registries.

medication.summary: A program that gives medicine needs an OCFS health care plan (approved by a health care consultant if it gives more than topical products and emergency medicines), and only designated staff who completed OCFS Medication Administration Training (or hold a nursing or medical license) may give it. Ongoing doses need written parent permission plus written instructions from the prescriber, medicine stays in its original container, each dose is documented, and errors must be reported to the parent immediately and to OCFS within 24 hours (18 NYCRR 418-1.11).

mandated_reporting.summary: Listed professionals must report, including day care center workers, school-age child care workers, family and group family day care providers, other child care workers, directors of overnight, summer day and traveling day camps, school staff, and compensated school employees who hold a coaching license or certificate (Social Services Law §413). Reports must be made immediately by phone, followed by a written report within 48 hours (§415).

child_care.agency: North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, Division of Child Development and Early Education (DCDEE)
child_care.licensing: DCDEE licenses child care centers and family child care homes. North Carolina's child care law covers regular care of three or more children under 13 for more than four hours a day by people who are not their relatives (G.S. 110-86). School-age programs and licensed summer day camps are licensed as centers under Section .2500 of the rules.
child_care.school_age_exemption: Programs operated by public schools are exempt. Seasonal recreational programs that run less than four consecutive months a year (summer day camps, typically May 15 to September 15) do not need a license, but must be licensed to serve children paid for by child care subsidy. After-school programs operating four hours a day or less are not required to be licensed. (G.S. 110-86; 10A NCAC 09 .2502; DCDEE guidance.)

camps.agency: County health departments (sanitation permits under NC DHHS environmental health rules); DCDEE for camps that choose or need a summer day camp license
camps.summary: North Carolina has no general youth camp license covering staffing or program safety. Summer camps that serve food or provide overnight lodging for pay need a sanitation permit and inspections from the local health department (15A NCAC 18A .1000; resident camps under .3600). Summer day camps running less than four consecutive months are exempt from DCDEE child care licensing unless they want to serve subsidized children, in which case they must be licensed as summer day camps (school-age children only).

background_checks.summary: Every child care provider (and household members 16 and older in home-based care) needs a DCDEE criminal background check qualification letter before starting work. The check covers federal and NC fingerprint databases, national and NC sex offender registries, an NC court records name check, the Responsible Individuals List, the Child Maltreatment Registry, and criminal, sex offender and abuse/neglect checks in any state lived in during the past five years. Letters are valid five years and must be renewed (G.S. 110-90.2; 10A NCAC 09 .2703). Unlicensed summer camps have no state background check requirement that we found.

medication.summary: No medicine, or even topical ointment, sunscreen or repellent, may be given without the parent's written authorization and written instructions. Prescriptions stay in the original pharmacy-labeled container, over-the-counter medicine stays in its original package labeled with the child's name (permission good for up to 30 days unless it is a standing authorization for chronic conditions or topicals), and every dose is recorded with the child's name, date, time, amount and the staff member's signature (10A NCAC 09 .0803). New staff get medication administration instruction during orientation (.1101).

mandated_reporting.summary: Any person or institution who suspects a child is abused, neglected or dependent must report to the county Department of Social Services where the child lives or is found, by phone, in person or in writing (G.S. 7B-301). Separately, any adult who knows or should reasonably know a child is the victim of a violent or sexual offense or misdemeanor child abuse must immediately report to local law enforcement (G.S. 14-318.6).
mandated_reporting.hotline: No statewide hotline; call the county Department of Social Services and ask for CPS intake (911 in an emergency)

child_care.agency: North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), Early Childhood Licensing
child_care.licensing: A license is required to care for more than five children, or more than three under 24 months, in exchange for payment; smaller home providers may self-declare instead. License types are family child care, group child care (up to 30 children), child care centers (larger programs), preschools, and school-age child care programs for ages 5 through 11 (N.D.C.C. 50-11.1-02, 50-11.1-03). Programs run by a government entity self-certify compliance ('public approval') instead of getting a license.
child_care.school_age_exemption: Not considered early childhood services, so no license: care in a public or private school in grade 1 or above; approved school-based programs for children under 6; summer resident or day camps that serve no children under 6 for more than two weeks; sporting events, practices or physical activities supervised by an adult; short religious classes; and care of up to four hours while the parent is on the same premises (N.D.C.C. 50-11.1-02(6)).
child_care.ratio_rule: N.D. Admin. Code 75-03-10-08(2)(a) (child care centers); 75-03-11.1-09 (school-age child care programs)

camps.summary: North Dakota has no youth camp licensing law that we could find. Summer resident or day camps are excluded from child care licensing as long as they serve no children under 6 for more than two weeks (N.D.C.C. 50-11.1-02(6)(g)); a camp that serves younger children longer than that may need a child care license.

background_checks.summary: Owners, staff, and volunteers or support staff who may be alone with children need a check approved before any unsupervised access: an FBI fingerprint check, national and state sex offender registry searches, state criminal history, ND child abuse and neglect records, and criminal, sex offender and abuse/neglect checks in any state lived in during the past five years. Center owners and staff must submit a fingerprint-based check at hire and at least every five years (N.D. Admin. Code 75-03-10-27, 75-03-10-28; N.D.C.C. 50-11.1-06.2). No camp-specific requirement was found.

medication.summary: Centers need written parent permission and proper instructions before giving any medicine; prescription medicine must come with the medical provider's written dosage and storage instructions and be labeled with the child's name and date. Medicine is stored out of children's reach (refrigerated medicine kept together in a spillproof container), and every dose, including over-the-counter, is logged with date, time, dosage, child's name and the staff member's name and kept in the child's record (N.D. Admin. Code 75-03-10-26(7)).

mandated_reporting.summary: Listed professionals must report when they learn of suspected abuse or neglect through their work, including child care workers, schoolteachers, administrators and counselors, medical and mental health professionals, social workers, foster parents, law enforcement, clergy and child care licensors; anyone else may report (N.D.C.C. 50-25.1-03). Reports must be made immediately, orally or in writing, with a written follow-up within 48 hours if requested (50-25.1-04).
mandated_reporting.hotline: 1-833-958-3500 (Child Abuse & Neglect Reporting Line, weekdays 8 a.m.-5 p.m. Central); call 911 if a child is in immediate danger

child_care.agency: Ohio Department of Children and Youth (DCY)
child_care.licensing: DCY licenses child care centers (care for seven or more children at one time), Type A and Type B family child care homes, and school-based preschool and school-age programs. Child care rules moved from the Department of Job and Family Services to DCY and were renumbered from OAC 5101:2 to 5180:2 (centers: Chapter 5180:2-12).
child_care.school_age_exemption: Child day camps (school-age children only, up to 12 hours a day and no more than 15 weeks in summer) are not licensed as child care; they register with DCY each year unless exempt under ORC 5104.21. Other licensing exemptions in ORC Chapter 5104: Not confirmed.

camps.agency: Ohio Department of Children and Youth (child day camp registration); local boards of health (resident camp permits under Ohio Department of Health rules)
camps.summary: Child day camps must register with DCY every year (by March 14) and pay a fee unless they meet an exemption in ORC 5104.21; camps that want to serve publicly funded children must also be accredited by the American Camp Association (or another DCY-approved body) and become DCY 'approved' day camps. Resident (overnight) camps need an annual permit from the local board of health and inspections under OAC Chapter 3701-25.

background_checks.summary: Center owners, administrators, employees and child care staff submit a request in the Ohio Professional Registry and get BCI and FBI fingerprints; DCY then reviews five checks: BCI, FBI, national sex offender registry, Ohio sex offender registry, and Ohio child abuse and neglect records (SACWIS). Checks must be redone every five years, after a six-month gap in child care work, or when joining a new program (new fingerprints not needed then). Registered day camps must run BCI and FBI checks before staff start and the camp administrator reviews results; approved day camps go through the full five-part DCY review.

medication.summary: Under the 2021 center rule, parents complete and sign a state 'Request for Administration of Medication' form for prescription and non-prescription medicine; a physician, dentist, APRN or PA must also sign instructions unless the medicine is in its original container with a current pharmacy or manufacturer label. The child must have had at least one earlier dose before the center gives any (except listed emergency medicines), medicine is stored out of reach in its labeled original container, each dose is documented on the form right away, and forms are good for up to 12 months (OAC 5101:2-12-25). This rule was replaced as OAC 5180:2-12-25 effective July 1, 2026.

mandated_reporting.summary: Ohio law lists required reporters by profession, including child care workers and day care staff, school employees and teachers, health professionals, clergy, social workers and children services staff (ORC 2151.421). Ohio is also among the states whose list covers directors, employees and volunteers of organized activities for children such as camps and recreation centers. Reports go to county children services or law enforcement.

child_care.agency: Oklahoma Human Services (OKDHS), Child Care Services – Licensing
child_care.licensing: OKDHS licenses child care centers (open 30 or more hours a week), part-day programs (more than 15 but under 30 hours a week), out-of-school time programs, day camps, drop-in programs, programs for sick children, and family and large family child care homes (10 O.S. §402; OAC 340:110-3-275). A program may not take children until OKDHS issues its permit or license (OAC 340:110-3-276).
child_care.school_age_exemption: 10 O.S. §403 exempts, among others: programs run by a public school district during typical school hours for children 3 and up; summer youth camps and summer or after-school programs for children 4 and up that are accredited by a national standard-setting or church camp accrediting body, or chartered by or affiliated with a national nonprofit; single-activity programs such as sports, art, music, dance, scouts and 4-H; programs open 15 or fewer hours a week, fewer than 10 weeks a year, or under 8 hours a day in summer; school-age-only center programs of 21 or fewer hours a week in counties under 100,000 people; drop-in programs with parents on site; and programs where children are not enrolled and come and go freely.
child_care.ratio_rule: OAC 340:110-3-286 and OAC 340 Appendix GG (Ratios and Group Sizes)

camps.agency: Oklahoma Human Services (OKDHS), Child Care Services (licensed day camps)
camps.summary: OKDHS licenses 'day camps' (run during school breaks, up to 12 hours a day, for children 5 and up who have attended kindergarten, outdoors at least half the day) unless the camp is exempt under 10 O.S. §403, for example accredited or national-nonprofit-affiliated camps, camps running under 10 weeks a year or under 8 hours a day in summer, and single-activity camps; summer resident (overnight) camps are exempt from child care licensing. A new law, HB 1675 (effective Nov. 1, 2026), requires all youth camps (day and overnight), camp facilities and outdoor programs to complete a severe-weather hazard assessment and emergency action plan by Jan. 1, 2027, file them with the county emergency management director, keep two weather-alert methods (one that doesn't rely on cell service), train staff every year, and give parents written notice of site hazards.

background_checks.summary: Owners, staff, and adults living in the facility need an OKDHS criminal history review before hire or unsupervised access: Oklahoma court records search, fingerprint-based national (FBI) check, sex offender registry, the Restricted Registry (Joshua's List), child abuse and neglect registries for any state lived in during the past 5 years, out-of-state criminal and sex offender checks when applicable, and two state caregiver abuse registries (10 O.S. §404.1; OAC 340:110-3-282). The review (without new fingerprints) is repeated every 5 years. Camps that are exempt from licensing are not covered by these licensing checks.

medication.summary: Parents supply the medicine and sign permission for each medication before it is given (up to 12 months at a time for chronic conditions). Only designated staff give it, from the original container labeled with the child's full name, following the label or a physician's instructions, never after it expires; each dose is logged right away, and medicines are kept out of children's reach except emergency medicines like epinephrine pens and inhalers, which stay near the child (OAC 340:110-3-295).

mandated_reporting.summary: Every person who has reason to believe a child under 18 is being abused or neglected must report it immediately to OKDHS through the statewide hotline (10A O.S. §1-2-101(B), as amended effective Nov. 1, 2025). Knowingly failing to report promptly is a crime, and school employees must also notify local law enforcement.

child_care.agency: Oregon Department of Early Learning and Care (DELC), Child Care Licensing Division
child_care.licensing: DELC certifies child care centers serving children from 6 weeks through age 12 (OAR 414-305) and school-age-only centers (OAR 414-310), and licenses family child care homes. Certain license-exempt preschool and school-age programs must still be 'recorded' with DELC.
child_care.school_age_exemption: Exempt from certification (OAR 414-305-0120): programs run by a school district, charter school, city, county or other government agency; single-enrichment activities such as sports practice, lessons or tutoring where no child attends more than 8 hours a week; group athletic or social activities of an organized club; care given only during summer or holiday breaks for fewer than 70 days a year; and youth development activities for school-age children when school is out. Programs offering youth development activities to school-age children must register as 'recorded programs': all staff and volunteers 18 and older enroll in the Central Background Registry and the program posts a notice for parents.

camps.agency: Oregon Health Authority, Public Health Division (or a delegated county health department)
camps.summary: Operating an 'organizational camp' requires a yearly license from the Oregon Health Authority or a delegated county health department; licenses expire Dec. 31 (OAR 333-030-0020). State law defines organizational camps to include youth, scout, summer, day, nature, survival and athletic camps, including those run by religious, school or community groups (ORS 446.310), and the rules cover sanitation, water, food service and camp health care. Separately, a school-age day program may need to be recorded with DELC or, if it works as child care, certified.

background_checks.summary: The operator, all center staff, and anyone 18 or older who may have unsupervised access to children must be enrolled in DELC's Central Background Registry (CBR) before working (OAR 414-305-0310). The CBR check covers Oregon State Police records, ODHS child protective services records, an FBI fingerprint check and sex offender registries, plus out-of-state checks for anyone who lived elsewhere in the past 5 years; enrollment expires every 5 years (OAR 414-061-0090). Recorded (license-exempt) school-age and preschool programs must also enroll staff and volunteers 18 and older. No separate background check rule for organizational camps was found.

medication.summary: Before giving any prescription or over-the-counter medicine, a center needs signed, dated parent authorization (up to 12 months for chronic conditions; phone permission is allowed for a single dose of a non-prescription medicine). Medicine must be in its original labeled container (prescriptions labeled with the child's name), not expired, given as labeled unless a physician writes otherwise; each dose is logged right away with any side effects, parents are told daily, and medicines are kept out of children's reach (OAR 414-305-1030).

mandated_reporting.summary: Oregon lists 'public or private officials' who must report immediately (ORS 419B.005, 419B.010), including school employees, registered or certified child care providers, operators of recorded programs, paid coaches and athletic trainers, and employees of organizations providing child-related services such as youth groups, scouts, and summer or day camps. Reports go to ODHS or law enforcement.

child_care.agency: Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, Office of Child Development and Early Learning (OCDEL), Bureau of Certification Services
child_care.licensing: A DHS certificate of compliance is required for child care centers (7 or more children), group child care homes and family child care homes (4 to 6 children) caring for children 15 and younger for part of a 24-hour day, including before- and after-school care in public or private, for-profit or nonprofit facilities (55 Pa. Code §3270.3).
child_care.school_age_exemption: Under an OCDEL policy statement (55 Pa. Code §3270.3a), part-day school-age programs for children in kindergarten through age 15 don't need certification if they run fewer than 90 consecutive days a year (most summer camps), operate 2 hours or less a day on 3 or fewer days a week, have a single focus such as basketball or art, are drop-in programs where children come and go, or are PDE-licensed or approved tutoring programs. A certified center that adds school-age children in summer doesn't qualify, and care during instruction hours in nonpublic schools is also exempt. OCDEL restated these rules for school-age programs in school buildings in Announcement C-26-01 (June 2026).

camps.agency: Pennsylvania Department of Health or the local (county or municipal) health department, for organized camp sanitation permits
camps.summary: Pennsylvania has no state program license for youth camps. An 'organized camp' (an outdoor group-living program run for 5 or more consecutive days) and campgrounds need a yearly sanitation permit covering water, sewage and toilets from the Department of Health or local health department (28 Pa. Code §§19.1, 19.11). School-age day camps (kindergarten and up) running fewer than 90 consecutive days are usually exempt from child care certification, but that exemption doesn't cover preschool-age children; camp employees and volunteers still need child abuse clearances.

background_checks.summary: Under the Child Protective Services Law, employees of child care and of any program, activity or service where they are responsible for children need three clearances: PA child abuse history, PA State Police criminal record, and an FBI fingerprint check, renewed every 60 months. Certified child care staff and volunteers also need a National Sex Offender Registry check and out-of-state checks if they lived outside PA in the past 5 years. Adult volunteers in youth programs need the child abuse and State Police clearances; the FBI check is needed only if they haven't lived in PA for the full past 10 years (otherwise a signed statement). Provisional hiring for up to 45 days is allowed under set conditions.

medication.summary: Centers must reasonably accommodate medication a child needs for a special need but are not required to give other medication. When they do: original container labeled with the medication and child's name, prescriber's written instructions for prescriptions (the label counts), written parent consent, locked or out-of-reach storage, and a medication log with dose, date, time and staff initials (55 Pa. Code §3270.133). Staff complete medication administration training within 90 days of hire (§3270.31(f)).

mandated_reporting.summary: Mandated reporters include school employees, child care employees with direct contact with children, and anyone, paid or unpaid, who as an integral part of a regularly scheduled program, activity or service is responsible for a child's welfare or has direct contact with children (23 Pa.C.S. §6311). They must report immediately to ChildLine by phone or online, then notify the person in charge of their organization.

medication.summary: No medication, prescription or over-the-counter, is given without written parent permission and a written order from a physician, PA or nurse practitioner (the pharmacy label can serve) in the original container. child_care.agency: South Carolina Department of Social Services (DSS), Division of Early Care and Education – Child Care Licensing
child_care.licensing: DSS licenses private child care centers (13 or more children) and group child care homes (7 to 12 children); government-run centers get DSS 'approval', and church-run centers that take no public child care money and family child care homes (6 or fewer) are 'registered' (S.C. Code §§63-13-20, 63-13-1010). State law defines childcare as care for more than 4 but less than 24 hours a day on more than two days a week.
child_care.school_age_exemption: S.C. Code §63-13-20(4) excludes schools operating solely for education in grade 1 and up; 5-year-old kindergarten; programs of 4 hours a day or less for children under school age; school vacation or holiday day camps run in sessions under 3 weeks (unless children can enroll in back-to-back sessions totaling more than 3 weeks); summer resident camps; and vacation Bible schools. Because 'childcare' means care for more than 4 hours a day on more than two days a week, school-age programs open 4 hours a day or less appear to fall outside licensing; confirm with DSS.

camps.agency: South Carolina Department of Social Services (only for day camps that don't qualify for the exemption)
camps.summary: South Carolina has no youth camp license: the former state health regulation for camps (Reg. 61-39) was repealed in 2016. Summer resident (overnight) camps are exempt from child care licensing, and school vacation day camps are exempt only if they run in sessions under 3 weeks and don't let children enroll in back-to-back sessions totaling more than 3 weeks; other day camps fall under DSS child care licensing (S.C. Code §63-13-20(4)(e)–(f)).

background_checks.summary: Before working in a licensed, approved or registered facility, caregivers and staff need a SLED state fingerprint check, an FBI fingerprint check, a DSS Central Registry of Child Abuse and Neglect check, and national (NCIC) and state sex offender registry searches, plus criminal, sex offender and child abuse registry checks in every state lived in during the past 5 years (S.C. Code §63-13-40(D)). Fingerprint checks are repeated every 5 years, or sooner if the person leaves child care for 6 months or more. Provisional hiring is allowed under strict supervision once the first checks clear.

medication.summary: Staff may give medication only with a signed, dated parent consent form good for no more than one year (an electronic authorization, or phone authorization for a single dose, is allowed), following the label or the health care provider's written changes, and never expired (S.C. Code §63-13-185). Medicines stay in the original labeled container with the child's first and last name and child-protective caps, are kept locked, and each dose is logged right away with a copy to the parent; medication errors must be recorded and parents told immediately (Regs. 114-505(D)).

mandated_reporting.summary: Listed professionals must report, including childcare workers in a childcare center, teachers, school counselors and principals, health and mental health professionals, clergy and law enforcement; anyone else may report and is encouraged to (S.C. Code §63-7-310). Reports go to the county DSS office or law enforcement; the statute does not set a specific deadline.

child_care.agency: South Dakota Department of Social Services (DSS), Office of Licensing and Accreditation – Child Care Licensing
child_care.licensing: DSS must license day care centers (21 or more children), group family day care homes (13 to 20 children) and before-and-after-school programs, regardless of funding source (SDCL 26-6-14). Family day care homes (12 or fewer children) register with DSS only if they are paid with public funds; others may register voluntarily (SDCL 26-6-14.1, 26-6-14.2).
child_care.school_age_exemption: Day care run by a school board for children of its enrolled students is exempt (SDCL 26-6-1.1). DSS says other before-and-after-school programs, including full-day care during school breaks, must be licensed whatever their location; the only exemption is a program offering educational or recreational activities where children come and go on their own.

camps.summary: No South Dakota youth camp licensing law was found. The Department of Health licenses campgrounds for the traveling public (ARSD 44:02:14), which is not a camp program license. A summer program that regularly cares for and supervises children may need a DSS child care license; DSS says school-age programs need a license even when they run full days during school breaks.

background_checks.summary: All child care providers and program employees 14 and older must meet federal background check requirements, repeated at least every 5 years (ARSD 67:42:17:13). In-state checks: South Dakota criminal records (fingerprints), state sex offender registry, the DSS child abuse and neglect central registry, NCIC, and an FBI fingerprint check; out-of-state criminal, sex offender and child abuse registry checks are required for each state lived in during the past 5 years. DSS pays the fees. No camp-specific requirement was found.

medication.summary: Before any medication is given, the parent's permission must be documented with the child's name, medication, dates, times and dosage. The parent supplies it in the original labeled container (prescription labels must show the child's name, dose and frequency, expiration date, prescriber and storage instructions); each dose is recorded with dose, time, date and who gave it, records are kept 6 months, medicines are stored out of children's reach, and unused or expired medicine goes back to the parent (ARSD 67:42:17:27–28).

mandated_reporting.summary: Listed professionals must report, including teachers, school counselors and officials, coaches of school activities, licensed or registered child welfare providers, employees and volunteers of child advocacy organizations or child welfare service providers, health professionals and law enforcement (SDCL 26-8A-3); the child care rules also require child care providers to report immediately (ARSD 67:42:17:47). Reports must be made orally and immediately to DSS, law enforcement or the county state's attorney (SDCL 26-8A-8); intentionally failing to report is a Class 1 misdemeanor.

child_care.agency: Tennessee Department of Human Services (TDHS), Child Care Services
child_care.licensing: A program needs a TDHS license if it provides care for 3 or more hours a day to 5 or more children who are not related to the caregiver. Family child care homes care for 5-7 children, group child care homes for 8-12, and child care centers for 13 or more (Rule 1240-04-01-.02; T.C.A. §71-3-501 et seq.).
child_care.school_age_exemption: Programs, such as after-school programs, that do not care for 5 or more unrelated children for 3 or more hours a day do not need a license. School-administered preschool and school-age programs are regulated by the Department of Education instead of TDHS. Other exemptions include recreational programs, camps that run only in summer (under 90 days a year) or only during school breaks, Boys & Girls Clubs, and YMCA school-age programs. Most exempt programs must register with TDHS, get written approval before operating, post a sign saying they are not licensed, and keep attendance records (T.C.A. §71-3-503, as amended July 1, 2025).

camps.agency: Tennessee Department of Health, Environmental Health Program (inspections by local health departments)
camps.summary: An organized camp needs a Department of Health permit before it opens (T.C.A. §68-110-103; Rule 1200-01-05). The permit covers health and sanitation, such as facilities, water, and sewage, rather than program staffing. The rules cover camps with outdoor group living or sleeping quarters and define a day camp as an organized camp program. Separately, a camp that meets the legal definition of child care is exempt from a TDHS license only if it runs in summer (under 90 days a year) or during school breaks, serves school-age children, registers with TDHS, and has written approval to operate (T.C.A. §71-3-503(b)(9)).

background_checks.summary: Owners, operators, directors, employees, substitutes counted in ratio who work more than 36 hours a year, and household members 15 or older need a fingerprint-based criminal background check and a registry review no more than 90 days before they have access to the agency. The registry review covers the Vulnerable Persons Registry, the sex offender registry, and Department of Children's Services abuse/neglect records. Checks must be repeated at least every 5 years and after a break in child care employment of more than 180 days. No one may have unsupervised contact with children until cleared (Rule 1240-04-01-.07; T.C.A. §71-3-507). We did not find a separate state background check requirement for youth camps.

medication.summary: A designated staff member must accept medication from the parent, get written parent authorization for each medication, and confirm that it is in its original container, not expired, and labeled with the child's name. Only staff trained in medication administration may give it, and each dose is documented (time, amount, side effects, staff name) with a copy to the parent. Medication is stored in a child-proof container, though emergency medications such as an EpiPen or inhaler may be kept unlocked out of children's reach (Rule 1240-04-01-.12(12)).

mandated_reporting.summary: Everyone in Tennessee is a mandated reporter and must report suspected child abuse or neglect immediately (T.C.A. §§37-1-403 and 37-1-605). Child care rules make each owner, director, staff member, substitute, and volunteer personally responsible for reporting. Staff may not wait to investigate first, and a program may not have policies that get in the way of reporting (Rule 1240-04-01-.10).

child_care.agency: Texas Health and Human Services Commission (HHSC), Child Care Regulation
child_care.licensing: Child-care centers, licensed and registered child-care homes, and listed family homes are regulated by HHSC under Human Resources Code Chapter 42. Programs that offer before- or after-school care or school-age program services are licensed under their own standards (26 TAC Chapter 744), which use the center ratios and group sizes.
child_care.school_age_exemption: Exempt programs include before/after-school programs run by (or under contract with) a school accredited by TEA or another recognized body, municipal recreation programs for ages 5-13 that meet city standards of care, neighborhood recreation programs, single-skill programs (such as sports or dance), short-term programs running less than 3 consecutive weeks and fewer than 40 days a year, programs where parents stay on the premises, and youth camps licensed by DSHS (26 TAC §§745.115-745.129; HRC §42.041(b)). Most of these exemptions come with conditions, such as telling parents the program is not licensed and running background checks.
child_care.ratio_rule: 26 TAC §746.1601 (ratios) and §746.1609 (maximum group size); 26 TAC §744.1601 and §744.1607 apply the same numbers to licensed school-age and before/after-school programs

camps.agency: Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS), Youth Camp Program
camps.summary: Day camps, resident camps, and travel camps that meet the state's youth camp definition need a DSHS youth camp license before operating (Health and Safety Code Chapter 141; 25 TAC Chapter 265, Subchapter B). A program counts as a youth camp only if it serves at least 5 minors away from their parents for 4 or more consecutive days, 4 or more hours a day, only during school vacations, for no more than 120 days a year, and offers at least two outdoor specialized activities such as swimming, archery, or horseback riding (25 TAC §265.11). A program that misses any of these criteria is not a youth camp but may need a child care license from HHSC. The Legislature rewrote the camp safety law in 2025 (HB 1 and SB 1), and DSHS adopted new rules in early 2026.

background_checks.summary: In licensed child care, staff and others who need a check must have a criminal history check (fingerprint-based for most staff), a check of the DFPS central registry of child abuse and neglect, a SEMARC check (misconduct findings held by HHSC's Employee Misconduct Registry, TEA, and the Texas Juvenile Justice Department), and, for child day-care operations, a National Sex Offender Registry check. People who lived outside Texas in the past 5 years also need out-of-state criminal, abuse/neglect registry, and sex offender registry checks. Fingerprint-based checks must be renewed at least every 5 years (26 TAC §§745.609-745.621). Licensed youth camps must run a criminal background check and a sex offender registry check on every adult staff member and adult volunteer before they have unsupervised contact with campers, and repeat both checks every year (25 TAC §265.12(f)).

medication.summary: Centers need the parent's authorization before giving any medication: in writing (signed and dated), electronically, or by phone for a single dose. An authorization expires after one year. Medication must be in its original container labeled with the child's full name, given as the label or the child's health-care professional directs, and logged with the child's name, medication, date, time, amount, and the staff member's name. Records must be kept 3 months (26 TAC §§746.3803-746.3809). A center that will not give medication must tell parents in writing before enrollment (§746.3811).

mandated_reporting.summary: Anyone who has reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused or neglected must report immediately. Professionals, including teachers, day-care employees, and anyone licensed by the state or working for a state-licensed facility who has direct contact with children, must report within 24 hours and cannot hand the duty to someone else (Texas Family Code §261.101).

unverified: The official text of Family Code §261.101(b) gives professionals 24 hours to report. The section was last amended in 2025 (SB 571), but we did not confirm which amendment changed it from 48 hours. Many older guides and training materials still say 48 hours.

The youth camp law (HSC Ch. 141) was substantially amended in 2025 (HB 1 and SB 1 after the July 2025 floods), and DSHS rules were updated in 2026. The fiber-internet requirement is in litigation. For the 2026 season, DSHS agreed not to deny or revoke licenses of camps that have redundant internet service, and the lawsuit is on hold until March 1, 2027. Check DSHS for current camp requirements before each season.

The HRC §42.041(b) subsection numbers for exemptions come from the HHSC handbook (effective July 1, 2025). A March 2025 rule adoption cited different subsection numbers, so the statute may have been renumbered.

child_care.agency: Utah Department of Health and Human Services, Division of Licensing and Background Checks (DLBC), Office of Licensing - Child Care
child_care.licensing: A child care center license is required to care for 5 or more unrelated children, for pay, away from the provider's or child's home, without the parent present, on an ongoing basis for 4 or more weeks a year (R381-100-3). An out-of-school-time license is required for programs that serve 5 or more children age 5 and older, for pay, 3 or more days a week and 30 or more days a year (R381-70-3). Home-based providers are licensed or certified separately.
child_care.school_age_exemption: No license is needed for care that is part of a program run by a school regulated by the state or local boards of education, or for care at a public school by an outside organization under contract with the school or with the school's oversight. Also exempt are nonprofit (501(c)(3)) programs for children over 4 and under 13 run under a written agreement with a city or county that oversees them, summer camps on federal land under a federal permit, and short, sporadic care (under 4 hours) with the parent in the building (Utah Code §26B-2-405; R430-8-4). Exempt programs must apply each year to verify their exempt status, post a notice that they are not licensed, and, except school-run programs, submit fingerprint background checks for staff (R430-8-5).
child_care.ratio_rule: Utah Admin. Code R381-100-10, Table 1 (child care centers); R381-70-10 (out-of-school-time programs: 1 staff per 20 children, maximum group 40)

camps.agency: Local health departments, under the DHHS Recreation Camp Sanitation rule (R392-300)
camps.summary: We found no state youth camp license in Utah. Camps used for temporary overnight stays must meet the state Recreation Camp Sanitation rule (R392-300), which covers water, sewer, and facilities and is enforced by the local health department. That rule does not set staffing or program standards. A day camp or other summer program that cares for 5 or more children age 5 and up, 3 or more days a week for 30 or more days a year, may need an out-of-school-time child care license unless it qualifies for an exemption, such as a summer camp on federal land under a federal permit or a nonprofit program run under a city or county agreement (R381-70-3; Utah Code §26B-2-405).

background_checks.summary: Before a new staff member or other covered individual starts, the provider must confirm their eligibility in the licensing provider portal. Anyone not already cleared submits an online application and fingerprints (age 16 and older) for a check by the DHHS Office of Background Processing. The check covers criminal history, the Utah and national sex offender registries, and supported child abuse/neglect findings in the state Licensing Information System (LIS). A new check is required if the person has been away from a licensed program for more than 180 days, has lived outside Utah since the last check, or turns 18. Providers and staff must report any new arrest, charge, or finding within 48 hours (R381-100-8). License-exempt programs, except school-run ones, must also submit these checks (R430-8-5).

medication.summary: Parent-supplied medication must be in its original or pharmacy container, with the original label and the child's full name. A signed, dated parent permission form must list the medication, dose, times, how it is given, and the condition being treated. Medication supplied by the center needs parent consent each time it is given. Staff record the date, time, dose, and any error or reaction, and must tell the parent about errors or reactions right away. Medication must be locked or stored out of reach (48 inches up, or 36 inches if refrigerated), and records are kept for 6 weeks (R381-100-17).

mandated_reporting.summary: Any person who has reason to believe a child is being or has been abused or neglected must immediately report it to the Division of Child and Family Services or the nearest law enforcement agency (Utah Code §80-2-602). Narrow exceptions exist for certain clergy confessions and attorney-client information.

child_care.agency: Vermont Department for Children and Families (DCF), Child Development Division (CDD), Child Care Licensing
child_care.licensing: Any place or program run regularly to care for and supervise children outside their homes for less than 24 hours a day needs a DCF license, or registration for a family child care home, unless it is exempt (33 V.S.A. §§3502, 3511). Vermont has separate license rules for Center Based Child Care and Preschool Programs, Afterschool Child Care Programs, and family child care homes.
child_care.school_age_exemption: Exempt programs include recreation programs that run less than 4 hours a day and no more than 13 weeks a year for children ages 3-5, or no more than 13 consecutive weeks for children who have finished kindergarten. Also exempt are programs that meet only 4 hours one day a week or 2 hours two days a week, single-skill activities, and programs run mainly for recreation where care is only incidental. A school-age program funded by 21st Century Community Learning Centers and overseen by the Agency of Education is exempt unless it takes child care subsidy (33 V.S.A. §3502(b); Afterschool Regulations ASP 1.5).
child_care.ratio_rule: Licensing Regulations for Center Based Child Care and Preschool Programs, CBCCPP 6.2.1.3 (Code Vt. R. 13-171-004); Afterschool Child Care Programs ASP 6.2-6.3 (Code Vt. R. 13-171-003)

camps.agency: Vermont Department of Health, Food and Lodging Program
camps.summary: Residential (overnight) children's camps that run 5 or more consecutive days and supervise children around the clock need an annual Department of Health license (18 V.S.A. §4351; Licensed Children's Camps Rule, effective 1/1/2018). The license covers sanitation, facilities, and health. We found no state license for day camps. A day camp that provides child care may need a DCF child care license unless it qualifies as an exempt recreation program, for example one that runs no more than 13 consecutive weeks for children who have finished kindergarten.

background_checks.summary: Before working with children, new staff, auxiliary staff, and others regularly present must submit a Records Check Authorization form to the Division. Staff and the licensee's representative must also be fingerprinted. No one may be left alone with children until the Division approves them based on a check that includes fingerprints. People on a sex offender registry, people with substantiated child abuse/neglect reports, and people with certain convictions are barred (CBCCPP 7.2). Staff must repeat the records check at least every 5 years (CBCCPP 2.3.9.3). We found no background check requirement in the Health Department's children's camp rule.

medication.summary: Only staff who have completed a Division-approved medication course may give medication, and only with the parent's written permission for each medication. The permission must list the child, date of birth, allergies, drug, dose, time, route, reason, start and end dates, and any special instructions. Prescription and over-the-counter drugs must be in their original, labeled containers and not expired. Each dose is logged, and records are kept 365 days. Rescue medications such as EpiPens and inhalers must be kept immediately accessible (CBCCPP 5.6).

mandated_reporting.summary: Mandated reporters include child care workers, school employees, camp owners, administrators, and counselors (at both residential and day recreation programs), health care providers, clergy, and other listed professions. They must report suspected abuse or neglect to DCF within 24 hours. Anyone else may report (33 V.S.A. §4913).
