child_care.agency: Virginia Department of Education (VDOE), child care licensing under State Board of Education regulations
child_care.licensing: A child day center needs a VDOE license if it cares for 2 or more children under 13 in a building that is not anyone's home, or for 13 or more children at any location. This includes short-term programs such as summer day camps (8VAC20-780-10; Code of Virginia Title 22.1, Chapter 14.1). Home-based child care is licensed separately.
child_care.school_age_exemption: No license is needed for single-focus instruction such as sports clinics or music, as long as no child under 6 attends and no child attends more than 25 days in 3 months. Also exempt are recreation or instruction programs within weekly hour limits (for example, no more than 6 hours a week for school-age children while school is in session), organized competitive sports leagues, programs where school-age children may come and go freely under a signed parent policy, and programs that run no more than 20 days a year. Local-government recreation programs for school-age children staffed by government employees, school-division programs staffed by division employees, and out-of-school-time programs affiliated with a national organization that meet set conditions are exempt too. Most exempt programs must file an annual notice with VDOE, tell parents in writing, post a notice, and report serious injuries (Code of Virginia §22.1-289.030).

camps.agency: Virginia Department of Health (VDH), Environmental Health (overnight camps); VDOE (day camps licensed as child day centers)
camps.summary: Overnight summer camps that host 12 or more unrelated minors overnight for any part of more than 2 consecutive days must have a VDH permit and are inspected each year by the local health department. The permit covers water, sewage, grounds, pools, and food (Code of Virginia §§35.1-1, 35.1-18; 12VAC5-440). Day camps are child day programs and need a VDOE child day center license unless they qualify for an exemption, for example a local-government recreation program or a program that runs no more than 20 days a year (Code of Virginia §22.1-289.030). VDH says its summer camp regulations are being updated.

background_checks.summary: All employees and volunteers at licensed child day centers, and at centers exempt under the religious exemption, must have a background check before starting and every 5 years after. The check includes a sworn disclosure, fingerprint-based state and FBI criminal history, a search of Virginia's child abuse and neglect central registry, and criminal, sex offender, and abuse registry checks in any state lived in during the past 5 years. People with a barrier crime or a founded abuse/neglect complaint may not work or volunteer. A new hire may start under supervision once their fingerprint check comes back clear, while other results are pending (Code of Virginia §22.1-289.035). Exempt out-of-school-time programs affiliated with national organizations must also run these checks (§22.1-289.030(B)(11)).

medication.summary: A center may choose to give prescription medication, over-the-counter medication, or only emergency medication, and it must have a written policy. Every medication needs written parent authorization, which expires or must be renewed after 10 work days unless a physician authorizes long-term use. Medication must be labeled with the child's name, drug, dose, and times. Prescriptions must be in the original pharmacy container, and over-the-counter drugs in the original container with directions. Only staff 18 or older with approved medication administration training (MAT for prescriptions, retrained every 3 years) may give it. Medication is kept locked, and each dose, reaction, and error is logged and reported to parents right away (8VAC20-780-510; 8VAC20-780-245 J).

mandated_reporting.summary: Listed professionals must report suspected abuse or neglect immediately, and never later than 24 hours. The list includes anyone employed in a school or child day program, paid child care providers, coaches and other adults working with sports organizations, administrators and employees (18 and older) of day camps, youth centers, and recreation programs, and any adult employed by or associated with an organization responsible for children (Code of Virginia §63.2-1509). Reports go to the local department of social services or the state hotline. Starting July 1, 2027, reports must go to the state hotline.

child_care.agency: Washington State Department of Children, Youth, and Families (DCYF)
child_care.licensing: DCYF licenses child care centers and family homes (up to 12 children) under Chapter 110-300 WAC, and school-age programs under Chapter 110-301 WAC. An agency that regularly provides early learning or child care for less than 24 hours needs a license unless the law excludes it (RCW 43.216.010).
child_care.school_age_exemption: Excluded from licensing are seasonal camps, meaning programs that run 3 months or less in any 12-month period and focus mainly on closely supervised recreation or education. Also excluded are programs run by any unit of local, state, or federal government (such as a school district or parks department), schools that accept only school-age children, and drop-in recreation or education programs for school-age children run by a local affiliate of a national nonprofit that follows the national group's safety standards. Programs where parents stay on site are also excluded (RCW 43.216.010(2)). Exempt school-age programs must report their exempt status on a DCYF form (WAC 110-301-0025).

ratios.ages: School-age (5-12, in kindergarten or elementary school)

camps.agency: Local health jurisdictions, under State Board of Health camp rules (Chapter 246-376 WAC)
camps.summary: Washington has no youth camp license. Seasonal camps (3 months or less a year, mainly recreational or educational) are excluded from DCYF child care licensing (RCW 43.216.010(2)(g)). Group camps that provide food and lodging must register each year with the local health officer at least 30 days before opening and meet State Board of Health sanitation and site rules (WAC 246-376-010 and -020). Those rules were last updated in 1997.

background_checks.summary: Licensed providers, staff, volunteers, and family-home household members must pass a DCYF background check before having unsupervised access to children, and repeat it at least every 3 years (WAC 110-06-0040; WAC 110-300-0105). The check includes fingerprints, an interstate check for every state lived in during the past 5 years, and disclosure of convictions, pending charges, and 'negative actions' such as founded child abuse or neglect findings. Fingerprints must be redone at renewal only if the person has lived outside Washington since the last check. We found no state background check requirement for seasonal camps, which are excluded from licensing.

medication.summary: Staff may give medication only after completing the program's medication orientation and DCYF's standardized medication administration training. They also need written, signed parent consent and must follow the label. Prescriptions must be for that child and labeled with the child's name, prescriber, dose, and duration. Over-the-counter medication must be in its original packaging, labeled with the child's name, and come with an authorization form. Every dose goes in a medication log (name, drug, dose, date and time, side effects, and the signature of the person giving it), and medication must be stored out of children's reach (WAC 110-300-0215).

mandated_reporting.summary: Mandated reporters include licensed or certified child care providers and their employees, school personnel, DCYF employees, clergy, nurses, and other listed professions. Supervisors at any nonprofit or for-profit organization must also report abuse by someone they supervise who coaches, trains, teaches, or has unsupervised access to children. Reports go to law enforcement or DCYF at the first opportunity, and no later than 48 hours (RCW 26.44.030).

Every out-of-school-time program, exempt or not, must register with DoHS when it opens and every year after (§49-2-113(h)).

camps.agency: Local health departments, under the WV Bureau for Public Health, Office of Environmental Health Services (sanitation permit for organized camps)
camps.summary: West Virginia has no youth camp license. Organized camps (places that give children or adults an outdoor group-living experience or have sleeping quarters) need an operating permit from the local health officer under the General Sanitation rule, with plan review for new or remodeled facilities and an inspection before the permit is issued (64 CSR 18 §§64-18-2, 64-18-3). Summer recreation camps with sessions of 30 days or less are exempt from child care licensing (W. Va. Code §49-2-113(e)(3)), and day camps run by county parks and recreation commissions or municipalities can be exempt if they meet the §49-2-113(e)(8) conditions.

background_checks.summary: Licensed centers must have a state and FBI fingerprint-based check run through WV CARES on every staff member and volunteer, and no one may work with children until WV CARES issues a fitness determination; staff stay enrolled in Rap Back for ongoing alerts. Centers must also check sex offender registries and child abuse and neglect registries in West Virginia and in every state lived in during the past 5 years, repeating the abuse registry search every 5 years (78 CSR 1 §8.4). There is no separate camp rule, but out-of-school-time and county parks and recreation or municipal camp programs claiming the §49-2-113(e)(8) exemption must run state and federal checks on all staff and volunteers.

medication.summary: Centers may give medicine only with the parent's written, signed instructions (child's name, medicine, reason, dose, time and route) and, except for limited over-the-counter use, a prescription or written order from a licensed health care provider; prescription medicine must be in its original pharmacy-labeled package, and medicine is kept in a locked container out of children's reach (sunscreen, diaper ointment and emergency medicine need not be locked but must be out of reach). Only staff who have passed approved medication administration training may give it, each dose is recorded in ink in a cumulative medication log, and medication errors must be reported to the director and parent (78 CSR 1 §§8.6.g, 15.4.h).

mandated_reporting.summary: Listed professionals must report, including child care workers, teachers and other school staff, youth camp administrators and counselors, and employees, coaches and volunteers of groups that run organized activities for children. They must report to DoHS immediately and within 24 hours at most, also report to the State Police and local law enforcement when serious physical abuse or sexual abuse is suspected, and tell the person in charge of their program; anyone else may report (W. Va. Code §49-2-803).

child_care.agency: Wisconsin Department of Children and Families (DCF), Division of Early Care and Education, Bureau of Early Care Regulation
child_care.licensing: Anyone who cares for 4 or more children under age 7 for pay, for less than 24 hours a day, needs a DCF child care license (Wis. Stat. 48.65(1)). DCF licenses family child care centers (up to 12 children from August 1, 2026), group child care centers (13 or more from August 1, 2026) and day camps, and school-age programs in a licensed center follow the group center rules in DCF 251.
child_care.school_age_exemption: The license requirement only covers care of children under 7, so a program serving only children 7 and older does not need a license (Wis. Stat. 48.65(1)). Also exempt: public, parochial and tribal schools, and counties, cities, villages, towns, school districts and libraries running programs mainly for recreation or social purposes (48.65(2)); DCF 251.02 also excludes programs of 4 hours a week or less, group lessons and athletic activities, and seasonal programs of 10 days or less in any 3-month period. School-run programs that want Wisconsin Shares subsidy or YoungStar must be monitored by DCF against part of DCF 251.

camps.agency: Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection (DATCP) and its agent local health departments for overnight recreational and educational camps; DCF for licensed day camps
camps.summary: Overnight camps (recreational and educational camps with overnight living quarters and planned group programs) need an annual license from DATCP or its agent local health department, whether free or fee-based (Wis. Stat. 97.67; ATCP 78.03, 78.07). Day camps caring for 4 or more children under 7 need a DCF day camp license under DCF 252, which covers seasonal, outdoor-oriented programs for children 3 and older. Day camps run by a county, city, village, town, school district or library mainly for recreation are exempt by statute, as are seasonal programs of 10 days or less in any 3-month period (DCF 252.03).

background_checks.summary: Every caregiver, non-caregiver employee and household member (age 10 and up) at a licensed center or DCF-licensed day camp needs a DCF child care background check before starting: Wisconsin criminal history, an FBI fingerprint check, national and Wisconsin sex offender registries, Wisconsin abuse and neglect findings and caregiver misconduct registry, and criminal, sex offender and child abuse registries in any state lived in during the past 5 years. Fingerprints must be redone every 5 years (Wis. Stat. 48.686; DCF 13). DATCP-licensed overnight camps must have applicants disclose sexual criminal history and consent to a check, review the national sex offender public registry before hiring, and adopt a policy barring people with listed offenses (ATCP 78.26(1)).

medication.summary: Staff may give prescription or over-the-counter medicine only with a dated, parent-signed authorization on file listing the child's name and birth date, the medicine, instructions, dosing interval and how long it lasts; blanket authorizations longer than the label allows are not permitted. Medicine must be in its original container labeled with the child's name, dose and directions, stored out of children's reach (refrigerated medicine in a separate labeled container), and given as labeled; new staff orientation must cover medication administration (DCF 251.07(6)(f); DCF 251.05(4)(a)6.).

mandated_reporting.summary: Listed professionals must report, including child care workers in child care centers, child care providers, teachers, school administrators, school counselors and other school employees, social workers, nurses and police (Wis. Reporters must tell the county child protective services agency (DCF in Milwaukee County) or the sheriff or local police immediately, by phone or in person (48.981(3)(a)1.); licensed day camp staff and volunteers must also report immediately and get yearly abuse-reporting training (DCF 252.07(3)).

License types are family child care homes (up to 10 children in the owner's home), family child care centers (up to 15) and child care centers (16 or more, in a non-residential building) (Ch. 11 §2(a)).
child_care.school_age_exemption: Exempt are after-school programs that operate mainly when school is out (before and after school and in summer), serve only children of compulsory school age, are organized for learning, youth development, enrichment, recreation or character-building, and follow local health, safety and fire codes (W.S. 14-4-102(b)(x)). Programs run or supervised by the state, a local government or a school district fall outside the definition of a child caring facility (W.S. 14-4-101(a)(vi)), and summer camps run by nonprofits are exempt (14-4-102(b)(viii)).
child_care.ratio_rule: Wyoming DFS Child Care Licensing Rules, Ch. 11 §2(b) (rules updated April 2026)

camps.summary: Wyoming has no youth camp licensing law in its statutes. Summer camps run by nonprofit organizations are exempt from DFS child care licensing (W.S. 14-4-102(b)(viii)), but a for-profit day camp caring for more than two unrelated children may need a DFS child care license unless another exemption applies, such as the after-school and summer program exemption for children of compulsory school age (14-4-102(b)(x)). 'Ranches for children', including summer-only ranches, are listed as child caring facilities that need DFS certification (W.S. 14-4-101(a)(vi)(J)).

background_checks.summary: Before working, owners, directors, staff, substitutes, volunteers present during operating hours, and household members 18 and older need a Central Registry (child abuse and neglect) check in Wyoming and every state lived in for the past 5 years, national and state sex offender registry checks, an FBI fingerprint check, and state criminal history checks (Ch. 11 §3(g)). The Central Registry and Wyoming sex offender checks repeat every year, and the FBI, state criminal and national sex offender checks repeat every 5 years. No state background check requirement for youth camps was found.

medication.summary: Staff may give medicine only after DFS-approved preservice training that includes medication administration, renewed every 2 years, and with written parent permission for each prescription or over-the-counter medicine (child, medicine, dose, instructions, date and time; for 'as needed' medicine the parent must be called that day first). Prescription medicine must keep its original label, be stored with child-safety caps out of children's reach, and be logged; parents are told the same day, and errors or reactions must be reported to the parent and Licensing within 24 hours (Ch. 11 §17).

mandated_reporting.summary: Every person who knows or has reasonable cause to suspect a child is abused or neglected must report immediately to DFS (the local child protective agency) or local law enforcement (W.S. 14-3-205). Staff of a school, facility or agency must also tell the person in charge, who then also has to make sure a report is made.
mandated_reporting.hotline: No single statewide number published: call the local DFS field office (listed on the DFS contact page) or local law enforcement; 911 in an emergency
